subtitle: A request or disagreement can be expressed in different ways. Learn to recognize it even when the wording is unfamiliar, then clarify the meaning with care and honesty.
scope: For staff across DHS. Original practice exchanges and private reflection examine direct and indirect communication without country profiles or personal labels. The course does not infer an IDI orientation, prescribe a single respectful style or change agency authority. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
introTranscript: A person can ask for a change plainly or convey it through a question, observation or explanation. Either form may be understood or missed. This course explores how two people interpret feedback during a practice neighborhood art gathering, then considers a separate DHS review exchange. You can work with the example or reflect privately on a familiar meaning without entering personal information.

intro.heading: Distinguish the words from the intended request
intro.body:
John Searle’s original discussion of indirect speech acts examines how a speaker can convey one purpose by expressing another. His account considers wording, shared information and inference. This course uses that conceptual distinction for its own practice exchanges; it does not turn a philosophical explanation into a rule about a nationality or an employee.

At a practice neighborhood art gathering, Mira and Noel are preparing a small display of their own prints. Mira says, “The window light is falling right on the darker print.” That is an observation. It might also be an indirect request to move the print, but the words alone do not tell Noel whether Mira wants a change, is explaining an effect or is simply noticing the light.

A more direct request would name the intended action: “Could we move my darker print away from the window?” It still leaves practical questions, such as whether the other space works. Directness does not guarantee that the request is feasible or that Noel agrees.

Noel can ask, “Are you suggesting that we move it, or are you pointing out how the light changes it?” This checks a particular purpose without describing Mira as evasive or demanding. The same person might use different forms when offering a comment, requesting assistance or setting a firm limit.

For learning, notice the difference between interpreting a message and assigning a personality. You can use Mira’s practice comment without drawing conclusions about anyone in your life.

flashcards.back: Wording that states the intended request, disagreement or other purpose more explicitly.
Wording that conveys a purpose through another statement, question or explanation, with context helping the listener interpret it.
What the words state on their own; this may not include everything the speaker intends.
A reading of the message that can be checked rather than treated as certain.
A question that checks the relevant meaning without judging the person’s character or demanding cultural disclosure.
A real limit that remains clear even when a response is expressed gently.

items.title: Name the literal observation
items.body: The comment describes light falling on the print. Calling it an observation accurately identifies the words, but does not settle their additional purpose. Noel can hold that distinction while asking what Mira wants to do.

items.title: Recognize a possible request
items.body: Moving the print could respond to Mira’s concern, but Noel has not yet heard a confirmed request. Acting immediately might interfere with a display Mira wants to keep. A specific clarification avoids treating an inference as an instruction.

items.title: Avoid a character verdict
items.body: Indirect wording is not evidence that Mira is dishonest, just as a plainly stated request would not prove selfishness. The task is to understand this exchange. Character labels would make the person’s actual answer less important than Noel’s first impression.

tabs.label: Assume an instruction
tabs.body: Noel moves the print without asking. The action may fit Mira’s intention, but it could also change a display she was merely describing. Responding quickly is different from knowing what the message means.

tabs.label: Reject the form
tabs.body: Noel tells Mira to stop hinting and speak properly. This turns a possible ambiguity into a judgment about how someone should communicate. It may discourage clarification without resolving what the observation was meant to convey.

tabs.label: Check the purpose
tabs.body: Noel asks whether Mira is suggesting a move or describing the effect. Either answer remains possible, and Mira does not have to explain an entire personal history. The response makes the relevant meaning available before a change is chosen.

check.question: What can Noel accurately conclude from Mira’s first comment?
check.correct: It describes the light and may convey a request; the intended action still needs clarification.
wrong: It is definitely an order to move every print.
Indirect wording proves Mira is concealing her motives.
A direct request would automatically make moving the print possible.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The observation and possible request are distinct. Clarifying the intended action is more reliable than treating the form as a command or character test.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The comment does not order a change to every print. A possible indirect request does not establish concealed motives. A direct request could make the intended action clearer, but it would not establish feasibility or agreement. Check this message’s purpose.

items.text: The window light falls on the darker print.
Mira may want the print moved.
Mira is dishonest because she used an observation.
The comment names a particular lighting effect.
Mira may only be describing what the light does.
Noel can identify Mira’s entire communication style from one sentence.

responses: This makes room for the actual purpose without a character label.

lessons.transfer: Use this practice exchange or silently recall an ambiguous comment. No personal example or written note is required.

move.control: You can distinguish the words, your interpretation and a question that would help.
move.failure: An inferred request becomes an instruction or a character judgment without checking.
move.next: Ask about the particular purpose before deciding how to respond.

Private insight does not require a work result.

intro.heading: Examine the meaning of gentle feedback
intro.body:
Mira explains that she is suggesting a different position for her print. She adds that, in a community art group where she learned to share work, people often began with an observation and invited the artist to decide what it meant for the piece. She connects that practice with respect for the artist’s ownership. This is Mira’s account of a meaningful experience, not a script for every community group.

Noel learned a different expectation in a family repair workshop: naming the needed change plainly signaled that a person trusted the other to help. He interpreted Mira’s observation as background because, to him, a request would normally name the action. He can recognize this learned expectation without treating it as the only considerate form.

The difference concerns meaning, not only the location of a print. Mira wants room for her artistic judgment; Noel wants to understand how to help. Hearing these meanings lets them discuss a change without making either person the model everyone must imitate.

Mira can make the request clearer while retaining ownership, and Noel can ask a specific question without accusing her of avoiding honesty. Neither has to disclose private family details or agree that the other’s approach is best in every setting.

You may privately consider what direct feedback or an observation-based suggestion has meant in your own learning. The insight can help you understand a value such as trust, autonomy or care. That personal understanding is a legitimate result even if you choose no work application.

Which interpretation fits the accounts?
lessons.keyStatement: Understand what the form of feedback signifies to the people in this exchange.

items.title: Respect for ownership
items.body: Mira’s observation is intended to leave space for the artist’s decision. Once Noel hears that account, the form has a meaning beyond insufficient detail. A suitable clarification can preserve ownership instead of replacing it with an order.

items.title: Trust through a named action
items.body: Noel associates a plainly named action with confidence that another person can help. That meaning explains his initial reading without making it universally correct. He can notice why a familiar form felt natural while also understanding Mira’s approach.

items.title: A personal insight can stand alone
items.body: Recognizing a learned connection between feedback and trust may deepen self-understanding. A person can keep that insight private and use the practice case for activities. The learning need not produce a work record, reveal a family story or prove a measurable effect.

tabs.label: Flatten the difference
tabs.body: A learner says both simply want the print moved, so the meanings do not matter. This misses the difference between preserving ownership and signaling trust. The same action could still feel like an order or an ignored request.

tabs.label: Assign a group rule
tabs.body: A learner declares all community artists indirect and all workshop participants direct. The example describes two individual accounts, not a population pattern. Such a rule would discourage listening to a person whose meaning differs from the imagined category.

tabs.label: Hold both meanings
tabs.body: A learner explains Mira’s ownership meaning and Noel’s trust meaning without ranking them. The next response can make the action clearer while retaining choice. The learner can also recognize a familiar personal value without documenting it.

check.question: What does learning the two accounts add?
check.correct: It explains why the forms felt considerate or unclear to these people and supports a response that preserves the relevant meaning.
wrong: It proves that every artist must avoid direct requests.
It establishes that Noel’s family method is more honest.
It is useful only if a supervisor can measure a work improvement.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The volunteered accounts connect communication form to learned meaning. Understanding a personal value and responding thoughtfully are both worthwhile possibilities.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Mira’s account does not establish a rule for every artist. Noel’s familiarity with direct requests does not rank his method as more honest. Personal cultural understanding can be worthwhile without a supervisor’s measure or a completed work change.

items.text: An observation can leave the artistic decision with the maker.
Naming the needed action can signal trust in someone’s help.
Compare both accounts without assigning everyone a style.
Respect for ownership matters in this feedback exchange.
A plainly expressed request is familiar as considerate assistance.
Reflect silently on a personal value or use the example.

The insight is invalid unless entered in an employee record.
responses: Respect cannot be ranked from these forms alone.
This keeps the meanings the people describe visible without a group rule.
Private personal understanding does not require a personnel record.

lessons.transfer: Use the practice meanings or reflect privately on a value connected to feedback. You do not have to share or write an experience.

move.control: You can recognize a learned meaning and another person’s different account.
move.failure: A meaningful form is dismissed or turned into a rule for a whole group.
move.next: Explain the two meanings the people describe without ranking the people.

objectives: Revise a practice indirect suggestion into a clear request.
Distinguish honest choice from pressure disguised as optional wording.
Preserve the speaker’s purpose without demanding a single communication style.

Gentle wording must not conceal a real obligation.

intro.heading: Make a request clearer while retaining choice
intro.body:
Mira tries another version: “I would like to move my print away from the window. Could we compare the two available positions before I choose?” The request names the action and preserves the purpose she explained: retaining artistic ownership. It is more explicit without becoming an instruction about Noel’s character or method.

Noel can respond honestly: “We can compare those positions. The narrow frame will not fit on the smaller stand, but the other wall is available.” He names an actual constraint in the practice display rather than hiding it behind “whatever you want.” A choice that does not exist is not made real by kind wording.

They can also retain an observation-based opening. Mira might begin by describing the light and then add the intended request. A combination can work here because it supplies the action and preserves the meaning. The course does not prescribe directness for every conversation.

A person should not need to perform another person’s style to count as cooperative. The useful change is that Mira’s purpose is understood, Noel’s practical information is available and the remaining decision is described truthfully. They may still disagree about the best display.

In private learning, try either version using the practice print. Notice how wording can become clearer without discarding a valued way of relating to another person.

Distinguish honest choice from pressure disguised as optional wording.
Preserve the speaker’s purpose without demanding a single communication style.

lessons.keyStatement: State the needed action and the real choice honestly.

items.title: Name the request
items.body: The revised message identifies moving the print and comparing positions. Noel no longer has to infer the intended action from a lighting observation. The artistic choice remains with Mira in this practice arrangement rather than being silently transferred to the helper.

items.title: Keep the constraint visible
items.body: The smaller stand’s limit is relevant practical information. Concealing it would create a false choice and a later surprise. Naming it calmly allows Mira to consider the feasible positions without turning the constraint into a criticism of her preferred feedback form.

items.title: Adapt without performing a role
items.body: Mira need not become a permanently direct speaker, and Noel need not imitate her group’s feedback ritual. A particular message can combine observation, a named action and choice. The adjustment is useful because it addresses the meanings they supplied.

tabs.label: Pretend every choice exists
tabs.body: Noel says any placement is possible despite the stand’s limitation. This sounds agreeable but withholds information Mira needs. A later refusal may feel inconsistent because the earlier statement gave a misleading impression of freedom.

tabs.label: Require a correct style
tabs.body: Noel agrees to help only if Mira abandons observation-based feedback forever. This makes support depend on a personal style performance. It is unnecessary to understand the present request and disregards the meaning Mira explained.

tabs.label: Clarify action and limits
tabs.body: Mira names the proposed move, and Noel explains the actual display constraint. They can compare feasible positions while preserving Mira’s purpose. A clear message supports a real choice without promising that every preference can be satisfied.

check.question: Which revision preserves both clarity and honest choice?
check.correct: Name the proposed move, ask to compare feasible positions and explain the actual stand limitation.
wrong: Say every location is available even when it is not.
Require Mira to promise she will always communicate directly.
Change the display silently and call that cultural learning.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This supplies the action and relevant constraint while keeping the purpose of artistic choice visible.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Promising unavailable locations conceals a real limit. Requiring a permanent style change is unrelated to clarifying this request. Silently rearranging the display may ignore Mira’s purpose and does not demonstrate understanding of the meaning she supplied.

items.text: I would like to move my print and compare the available positions.
The narrow frame will not fit on the smaller stand.
Help depends on never using indirect wording again.
Could we look at the other wall before I choose?
The other wall is available in this practice display.
Call every option free while concealing a known restriction.

options: The display can be changed without discussing Mira’s purpose.
A friendly tone makes every option feasible.
The intended action, feasible choices and actual limitation can be stated together.
responses: This could replace ownership with an unrequested decision.
Tone does not change the physical limitation.
This combines meaning, clarity and truthful limits.

lessons.transfer: Try a revised request with the practice print or reflect silently on wording you value. No personal message needs to be submitted.

move.control: You can make an action clear without hiding a constraint or requiring imitation.
move.failure: Kind wording conceals pressure or becomes a condition on personal style.
move.next: State the request and the actual choice in the same exchange.

lessons.title: Recognize a possible refusal without demanding a personal account
lessons.summary: Distinguish an explanation from a confirmed response to an invitation.
lessons.objective: Distinguish an explanation from a confirmed response to an invitation.
objectives: Distinguish an explanation from a confirmed response to an invitation.

Separate relevant availability from unnecessary personal disclosure.
takeaways: An explanation may convey a decline.
Clarify the commitment rather than demand biography.
A genuinely optional invitation allows refusal.
lessons.statement: Make the response understandable while preserving the person’s choice and privacy.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Recognize a possible refusal without demanding a personal account
intro.body:
Noel invites Mira to help at another voluntary neighborhood gathering. Mira replies, “I have already promised to be with someone that morning.” The sentence describes a commitment. In this conversation it may also convey that she cannot attend. Noel can recognize that possibility without assuming whether the commitment concerns care, a celebration or another activity.

Mira explains only what she wants to: she learned to decline invitations by naming an existing commitment because it expressed regard for both relationships. Noel had heard the response as an opening to find a later time. Their different interpretations can be clarified without calling the explanation an excuse.

Noel can say, “I understand you are not available that morning. Would you like me to leave the invitation there?” That acknowledges a likely decline and gives Mira a choice about further discussion. If he is genuinely unsure, he can ask whether she is declining this invitation, rather than asking whom she will see or what duties she has.

An invitation a person can decline is different from a required work responsibility. The practice choice cannot be imported as permission to disregard an actual duty. Its lesson is about making the intended response available while avoiding pressure disguised as friendly persistence.

You can privately consider whether you tend to hear an explanation as a decline, negotiation or request for reassurance. Understanding that expectation can be useful in itself, without sharing a personal commitment.

Separate relevant availability from unnecessary personal disclosure.

lessons.keyStatement: Make the response understandable while preserving the person’s choice and privacy.

items.title: Keep the response question specific
items.body: Noel needs to know whether Mira is joining the gathering, not why her other relationship matters. A question about declining the invitation can resolve the practical ambiguity while leaving private details outside the exchange.

items.title: Do not manufacture negotiation
items.body: If Mira confirms a decline, proposing repeated alternatives may turn a free invitation into pressure. A later invitation could be welcome, but Noel should not assume that every explanation means “persuade me.” The supplied response matters more than a familiar conversational habit.

items.title: Separate the contexts
items.body: A voluntary neighborhood event allows a choice the organizer genuinely controls. Actual DHS responsibilities may have requirements and authorized processes. Understanding a gentle refusal can inform communication without making every work task optional or concealing a real obligation.

tabs.label: Demand proof
tabs.body: Noel asks for the other person’s identity and details to decide whether the commitment is good enough. This demands information unrelated to a voluntary invitation. It changes a choice into a test and overlooks Mira’s confirmed response.

tabs.label: Keep persuading
tabs.body: Noel treats every explanation as a request for more options and refuses to accept a decline. This may follow his familiar pattern, but it ignores what Mira says she means. The invitation is no longer experienced as genuinely optional.

tabs.label: Check and accept the response
tabs.body: Noel clarifies whether Mira is declining, accepts her answer and leaves personal details with her. He understands the commitment well enough for the invitation without demanding agreement about a universal refusal style.

check.question: What does Noel need to clarify for this voluntary invitation?
check.correct: Whether Mira is declining this invitation, without requiring the identity or private details of her other commitment.
wrong: Whether her other commitment deserves his approval.
Whether every future explanation from Mira means refusal.
Whether the same invitation makes all DHS duties voluntary.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The relevant response can be understood without private proof, a permanent label or a false work rule.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Noel does not need to approve Mira’s personal commitment for an optional event. One explanation does not establish every future meaning. The voluntary gathering does not change actual DHS duties. Clarify this response and preserve the choice that truly exists.

items.text: Is Mira declining this invitation?
Who is the person she promised to see?
The invitation is genuinely voluntary.
Does Mira want to discuss another date?
What personal duties make her commitment important?
The example does not waive a required work process.

responses: This respects the confirmed response and genuine choice.

lessons.transfer: Use the practice decline or consider your own interpretation privately. No personal schedule or relationship information needs to be recorded.

move.control: You can clarify a response without turning the person’s life into evidence.
move.failure: A gentle explanation invites repeated pressure or unnecessary disclosure.
move.next: Ask only what is needed to understand this invitation response.

lessons.statement: Make the concern, its reason and the actual responsibility clear.

intro.heading: Clarify a professional concern without inventing a requirement
intro.body:
In a separate practice DHS exchange, Ellis, who is checking the comparison, tells colleague Rowan, “The comparison would benefit from a clearer explanation of its basis.” Ellis intends to identify a limitation before the work goes through its actual review. Rowan hears a discretionary style preference and prepares to proceed unchanged.

Ellis explains that earlier learning emphasized offering a concern gently so the author could respond without feeling publicly diminished. Rowan explains a different expectation: if something must be addressed, the person checking the work normally says so plainly. These are volunteered individual accounts. They do not establish a style for every colleague, administration or community.

Ellis can state the concern directly: the present comparison does not identify what its figures describe. Ellis can then explain what is a request for clarification, what the actual review requires and who has the authority to decide readiness. The case does not authorize Ellis to invent a new agency requirement, approve a release or demand sensitive group data.

Rowan retains responsibility for the work and can ask about evidence or disagree with the concern through the appropriate process. Program consultation offers guidance and feedback rather than taking over the analysis. DHS’s relevant equity-analysis responsibilities continue to apply.

If the exchange also reveals an allegation or incident of protected-class harassment or discrimination, a manager or supervisor must immediately report it to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow agency procedures under MMB Policy 1436. Clarification, reflection and apology do not replace that responsibility or an authorized assigned investigation.

Adapt an explanation in light of a colleague’s supplied meaning of respectful feedback.
Retain actual staff ownership, review authority and reporting responsibilities.
Which response uses the meaning without changing authority?
lessons.keyStatement: Make the concern, its reason and the actual responsibility clear.

items.title: Explain the concern specifically
items.body: A comparison without a stated basis can be difficult to assess. Ellis should identify what is missing rather than rely on a polite phrase to carry the entire concern. This allows Rowan to respond to the reasoning instead of guess whether a vague suggestion is mandatory.

items.title: Identify the actual requirement
items.body: The real task and review process determine which steps are required. Ellis’s intended urgency does not create authority. Naming the actual responsibility separates optional presentation advice from a concern that must be addressed through the relevant process.

items.title: Let meaning change the explanation
items.body: Ellis understands that understated feedback may be read as optional, while Rowan understands its intended regard for authorship. Ellis can retain respectful tone and plainly identify the concern. This connects meaning to response without using an exchange as an individual IDC assessment.

tabs.label: Hide the distinction
tabs.body: Ellis repeats the gentle phrase and expects Rowan to infer every responsibility. This preserves a familiar form but leaves the concern’s status unclear. A later accusation of noncompliance would be unfair if the actual requirement was never accurately identified.

tabs.label: Invent authority
tabs.body: Ellis announces a new review rule and demands detailed personal group information to resolve it. That exceeds what the practice concern establishes. Clarity should expose actual responsibility, not create unsupported authority or disregard information-handling limits.

tabs.label: Explain concern and responsibility
tabs.body: Ellis identifies the missing basis and describes the real review role and next step. Rowan can respond with reasoning and retain ownership. The response changes in light of supplied meaning without promising a favorable result or bypassing required duties.

check.question: What is the stronger professional response?
check.correct: Explain the missing basis, distinguish the concern from optional advice and identify the actual review responsibility without inventing a rule.
wrong: Make the entire review optional so Rowan is comfortable.
Create a new data demand because indirect feedback was misunderstood.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Specific concern and actual authority can be made clear together. Staff ownership and legitimate disagreement remain intact.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Making actual review optional would change a responsibility rather than clarify it. Rowan’s reading does not establish dishonesty. A new data demand cannot be justified by misunderstanding alone and must respect actual authority, relevance and information-handling requirements.

items.text: The comparison does not state what its figures describe.
Follow the real task’s required review.
A single misunderstanding proves dishonesty.
The stated basis needs clarification for this comparison.
A manager immediately reports a protected-class allegation to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer.
Invent a new requirement or sensitive-data demand to make the point stronger.

move.failure: Indirect wording hides a requirement, or clarification invents authority.

intro.heading: Review understanding without demanding a universal style
intro.body:
Mira and Noel compare two positions, and Mira chooses the other wall for her print. They have clarified that her lighting observation was a request and that she wanted to retain ownership of the choice. They have also learned why observation-based feedback and a plainly named action felt considerate in their different experiences.

This does not show that everyone at the gathering now shares a communication style or that every future request will be understood. The useful result is narrower: the purpose of this request and the actual display choice became available. A new exchange may involve different meanings or constraints.

If Noel had moved the print without asking, he could acknowledge the particular gap: “I treated your observation as a decision before I checked what you wanted.” He can ask about a feasible repair without requiring Mira to reassure him, forgive the error or accept another unrequested move.

A learner may finish with a private insight about how trust or regard is expressed. Another may choose an appropriate work application such as explaining the status of feedback more clearly. Neither path requires recording personal histories. A useful application should remain within actual responsibility and information-handling practices.

There is no need to label someone direct or indirect forever. The ongoing practice is to listen for the particular purpose, check relevant meaning and state choices or constraints honestly. Understanding can deepen even when the people retain different ways of expressing care.

lessons.keyStatement: Describe what became clearer and leave wider effects open to actual evidence.

items.title: Name the specific result
items.body: The intended request and display choice are now clear in this case. Describing that result avoids turning a completed move into proof that every participant understood or that one style should govern every setting. Actual feedback can refine understanding later.

items.title: Acknowledge the actual gap
items.body: A repair should identify treating an interpretation as a decision. A vague apology for “culture” would obscure what happened. A specific acknowledgment permits a feasible correction while leaving Mira free to respond without supplying reassurance.

items.title: Keep more than one learning path
items.body: Personal understanding of a value such as ownership or trust can remain private. An optional work path can focus on a nonsensitive task and actual responsibility. Neither requires a record of someone’s cultural background or proof that all disagreement has disappeared.

tabs.label: Claim universal success
tabs.body: A learner concludes that everyone will communicate clearly because the print was moved. The event supports only a particular clarification and choice. Such a claim could make later confusion harder to acknowledge because it has already been declared solved.

tabs.label: Require personal proof
tabs.body: A learner demands cultural histories and written reflections to prove understanding. This adds disclosure pressure unrelated to clarifying the request. The practice activity and private insight are complete ways to learn without turning identity into a work record.

tabs.label: Review the exchange proportionately
tabs.body: A learner names what became clear, what changed and what remains unknown. They may keep personal insight private or try a suitable work application. A specific repair and honest limits preserve room for continued learning rather than certify a permanent style.

check.question: Which ending accurately describes the learning?
check.correct: The request and choice were clarified, the meanings became more understandable and wider effects remain open; private insight is also worthwhile.
wrong: Moving one print proves everyone has the same communication style.
A learner must disclose family history for the course to be meaningful.
A kind apology automatically closes any formal protected-class concern.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This describes the observed clarification and personal learning without unsupported wider claims or required disclosure.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One display choice does not establish a shared permanent style. Family history is not required; examples and private reflection are legitimate paths. An apology does not replace a manager’s immediate Policy 1436 reporting duty or the actual formal procedures.

items.text: Mira clarified that the lighting observation was a request.
All future requests will be understood.
Reflect silently on the meaning of considerate feedback.
The practice print was moved to the position Mira chose.
Everyone at the gathering now communicates the same way.
Try an appropriate nonsensitive work application or stay with the example.

lessons.next: You can revisit the practice exchanges or use the job aid privately. A particular meaning can become clearer while personal differences and continued learning remain.

scenario.context: Consider this situation: The print has been moved after the request and feasible choices were discussed.
scenario.prompt: What should the learner take forward?
options: A permanent label for Mira and Noel.
A claim that formal responsibilities are complete because everyone was polite.
A specific understanding of the request and meanings, with private reflection or an appropriate next practice.
responses: The case does not establish fixed personal types.
Politeness does not complete separate formal duties.
This preserves the real learning without a universal outcome claim.

lessons.transfer: Choose a private insight, the practice case or a suitable nonsensitive practice. No entered personal note or demonstrated work result is required.

move.control: You can review a particular exchange without certifying a person or a universal outcome.
move.failure: A helpful clarification becomes a permanent label or an unsupported success claim.
move.next: Name the clarified purpose and any actual change; keep unknown wider effects honest.

jobAid.subtitle: Understand the purpose, check the relevant meaning and respond honestly.
remember: A comment or question may also convey a request, but a possible reading is not a confirmed instruction.
Direct and indirect wording do not establish character, nationality or individual IDC orientation.
Personal cultural understanding may remain private and worthwhile without a work record.

sections.heading: Notice and check
items: Separate the supplied words from the purpose you infer.
Ask about the particular request, suggestion or decline rather than demand a personal cultural account.
Listen to a volunteered meaning of care, trust or ownership without turning it into a group rule.

sections.heading: Make the response understandable
items: State the needed action and any real constraint honestly.
Keep genuinely optional invitations and support distinct from actual responsibilities.
Do not make help depend on permanently adopting your preferred style.
Retain staff ownership and the task’s actual review and information-handling requirements.

sections.heading: Review or repair
items: Acknowledge treating an interpretation as a decision if that is the actual gap.
Describe the clarified meaning and observed change separately from wider effects not yet checked.
Use a practice example or an unrecorded private reflection; no personal story needs to be entered.
Managers and supervisors immediately report protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow actual assigned procedures.

sources.title: John R. Searle: Indirect speech acts
sources.note: The original 1975 chapter’s introductory discussion distinguishes wording and intended acts and considers shared information and inference. Its national or personal applications are not assumed here; all art and DHS exchanges are newly authored.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Conceptual education reference for personal cultural understanding, perspective-taking and communication. Private insight is worthwhile alongside appropriate practice; no source exercise is reproduced.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Actual staff equity-analysis responsibilities remain in place. Communication learning and consultant guidance do not transfer ownership or invent review authority.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1436: Harassment and discrimination prohibited
sources.note: Immediate manager and supervisor reporting and actual agency procedures remain distinct from clarification and apology. This course does not make a formal finding.
